newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain queries Portugal on refused ETA extradition.
newsitem.headline: Spain queries Portugal on refused ETA extradition.

text.p: Spain reacted with surprise on Thursday to the Portuguese Supreme Court's decision to free a suspected ETA supporter sought by Madrid and demanded an explanation from its neighbour.

Jose Luis Telletxea, accused by Spain of smuggling ETA Basque separatist rebels and weapons across the border with France, was released on Wednesday hours after winning his appeal against extradition, which had been ordered last month by a lower court.
"There will be government-to-government negotiations to ask what happened and to see if there is any possible appeal for this decision," a Justice Ministry spokesman told Reuters.
Portuguese newspapers said the latest ruling was based on a lack of evidence backing Spain's case.
But Spanish Justice Minister Margarita Mariscal said the case for extradition was solid, and blamed the decision to reject it on lack of coordination among Portugal's judicial bodies.
She called on all European Union states to harmonise their laws to make extradition easier.
"The disparate institutions are putting up a series of obstacles, or what could be interpreted as obstacles by the courts," Mariscal told state radio on Thursday.
She said Portugal's ruling was a surprise because Telletxea's extradition had been one of the topics at a bilateral summit in October and Portugal had agreed to cooperate.
Telletxea, 35, was living in Portugal in 1996 when he was arrested for trying to travel to Venezuela on false papers.

He was sentenced to six months jail for falsifying documents and his request for political asylum was refused. One day before he completed his term his sentence was increased by three months to enable Portugal to study Spain's extradition request.
For Spain, which has been battling ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) guerrillas for nearly 30 years, extradition is a highly sensitive topic and each case is potentially explosive.
A diplomatic row with Belgium erupted last year after Brussels' top judicial authority ruled against extraditing a couple suspected of collaborating in an ETA attack.
Belgium's decison to release the pair on political grounds was a slap in the face for Spain, which has demanded an end to the concept of political asylum within the European Union.
"No one is prosecuted for what they think in the EU, there is no political crime," Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said earlier in the week in Brussels.

He warned that Spain may refuse to sign a new Maastricht Treaty, which sets the guidelines for the European Union, unless it banishes the right to political asylum for EU citizens, a move human rights groups view with great concern.
ETA has killed some 800 people since starting a drive for Basque independence 30 years ago.
